approachQuestion.prompt: A token array contains exactly one valid prefix expression. An expression is an integer token, or the token DIFF followed by two expressions; DIFF means first minus second. Return the expression value. Examples: [DIFF,9,DIFF,5,2] returns 6; [DIFF,DIFF,9,5,2] returns 2; [7] returns 7.
constraints: There are n tokens, 1 ≤ n ≤ 100000, with expression nesting depth h ≤ 1000.
All arithmetic fits signed 64-bit integers; token reads and arithmetic take constant time.
The array is valid and read-only. A token slice copies all of its tokens.

options.text: Define parse(i) to return (value,nextIndex). An integer consumes one token; DIFF parses the first child at i+1, then parses the second at the first child's nextIndex.
options.feedback: The returned cursor identifies the second expression even when the first expression consumes many tokens.

options.text: Use the same parser but copy the entire remaining suffix at each recursive entry and translate consumed lengths back to positions.
options.feedback: It produces the same parse, but copies many tokens unnecessarily.

options.text: For DIFF parse its children starting at i+1 and i+2 regardless of the first child's size.
options.feedback: In [DIFF,DIFF,9,5,2], the second root child begins at index 4, not index 2.

options.text: Subtract every integer token after the first integer token, ignoring the expression nesting.

feedback.reason: The first child's returned cursor locates the second child; arithmetic cannot infer that boundary from token count alone.
details: parse(i) returns a value and the first index it did not consume. Integer tokens return their value and i+1. For DIFF call parse(i+1), then call parse at the returned cursor; return the first value minus the second and the second returned cursor. Begin at zero.

The first child's returned cursor locates the second child; arithmetic cannot infer that boundary from token count alone. Return the cursor after the complete expression to avoid reparsing or copying token slices.

“Define parse(i) to return (value,nextIndex). An integer consumes one token; DIFF parses the first child at i+1, then parses the second at the first child's nextIndex.”: The returned cursor identifies the second expression even when the first expression consumes many tokens.
“Use the same parser but copy the entire remaining suffix at each recursive entry and translate consumed lengths back to positions.”: It produces the same parse, but copies many tokens unnecessarily.
“For DIFF parse its children starting at i+1 and i+2 regardless of the first child's size.”: In [DIFF,DIFF,9,5,2], the second root child begins at index 4, not index 2.
“Subtract every integer token after the first integer token, ignoring the expression nesting.”: [DIFF,9,DIFF,5,2] means 9-(5-2)=6, not 9-5-2=2.

complexityQuestion.prompt: Analyze method-1 as described in the revealed method. Let n be token count and h expression depth. Calls share the array and pass indices; no slices are made. Count call frames, exclude input and scalar output; no tail-call elimination or hashing. Choose the tightest worst-case time and auxiliary-space pair among the options.

feedback.reason: Each prefix token is consumed once with one frame per pending operator.
details: Every token is consumed once. Each pending DIFF retains one cursor and at most one child result, bounded by nesting depth.
“O(n) time, O(1) auxiliary space”: Nested calls remain active along a path; their storage must be counted.
“O(n²) time, O(h + 1) auxiliary space”: Each object is processed once without rescanning or copying its descendants.
“O(h + 1) time, O(h + 1) auxiliary space”: A shallow but wide input can still require inspecting every object.
